II. BACKGROUND
The construction industry is recognized as one of the most
hazardous sectors worldwide, with workers facing elevated
risks of heat-related illnesses under extreme environmental
conditions [1]. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures and
humidity can lead to dehydration, heat exhaustion, and even
fatal heat stroke, while simultaneously reducing productivity
and increasing the likelihood of accidents due to impaired
cognitive and physical performance [6]. As climate change
intensifies, the frequency and severity of extreme heat events
continue to rise, emphasizing the urgent need for proactive
monitoring systems that extend beyond conventional safety
measures such as self-reporting or visual inspections [2].
Effective prediction and mitigation of heat stress rely on
monitoring key physiological indicators, including heart rate
(HR), heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rate, oxygen
saturation (SpO2), and core body temperature [1]. Recent
advancements in wearable biosensors provide an opportunity
for continuous, real-time tracking of these metrics in operational environments. Commercially available devices such as
smartwatches and chest straps have demonstrated the ability
to non-invasively capture relevant physiological data [4]. In
construction settings, wearable technologies have been used
to evaluate mental fatigue, ergonomic risk, and stress levels
during physically demanding or high-altitude tasks [3], [11],
[12]. Low-cost devices such as Garmin Vivosmart and Fitbit have been validated for field-level monitoring, offering
portability, cloud-based data integration, and scalability across
diverse worksites [4].
In parallel, deep learning techniques have increasingly been
applied to time-series physiological data to predict occupational health outcomes. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
networks are particularly effective in modeling sequential data
because they capture long-term dependencies that traditional
methods cannot [13]. In construction safety research, LSTM
models have been applied to predict fatigue using EEG signals
[6], classify ergonomic risks through posture recognition [14],
and monitor cognitive workload during simulated high-risk
operations [15]. Similarly, Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) have been employed for motion classification and fall
detection based on inertial sensor data [16]. While these models can achieve high predictive accuracy, their interpretability
is often limited, which challenges adoption in safety-critical
environments. To enhance transparency, attention mechanisms
have been integrated with LSTMs to identify the most influential features driving predictions, thereby improving both
accuracy and explainability [17], [18]. Combining physiological and environmental data through multi-modal approaches
has further improved predictive reliability, highlighting the
potential of integrated monitoring strategies in real-world
construction settings [19].
Despite these advancements, several limitations remain.
Many prior studies rely on small sample sizes or controlled
laboratory conditions, reducing their generalizability to operational worksites [4], [14]. Moreover, models often lack
interpretability, limiting trust and practical application in highstakes environments [14]. Few studies have specifically ad-

the present study collected real-world data from nineteen male
construction workers in Saudi Arabia over a five-month period
from June to October 2023, during the region’s hottest season.
Participants, engaged in routine physically demanding tasks
under direct sunlight, wore Garmin Vivosmart 5 smartwatches
integrated with the Labfront platform, continuously recording
heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration rate, oxygen saturation, and stress levels. These data provide a foundation for
developing an attention-enhanced LSTM framework capable
of accurately and transparently predicting heat stress under operational conditions. Table I summarizes representative studies

III. METHODOLOGY
This study adopted a methodological framework that included data collection, preprocessing, model development,
training, and evaluation. The primary objective was to capture
the physiological responses of construction workers under realworld heat exposure and to develop predictive models capable
of identifying early signs of heat stress with robustness and
generalizability, as shown in Fig. 2.
A. Data Acquisition
The dataset was collected at an active construction site in
Dammam, Saudi Arabia, between June and October 2023,
coinciding with the region’s most intense summer period.
Nineteen male workers between 35 and 40 years of age
voluntarily participated. The participants were engaged in
physically demanding tasks such as crane operation, excavation, structural assembly, and material handling, often under
prolonged direct sunlight. Physiological data were recorded
using Garmin Vivosmart 5 wearable devices connected to
the Labfront data acquisition platform. These devices continuously captured heart rate (HR), heart rate variability
(HRV), respiration rate (RR), oxygen saturation (SpO2), and
stress index during full work shifts. Portable sensors recorded
environmental conditions such as ambient temperature and
relative humidity in parallel. Work schedules were structured
as 8:00 AM–12:00 PM, followed by a mandatory rest period
from 12:00 PM–3:00 PM, and then resumed from 3:00 PM–
6:00 PM.

the integrity of physiological signals, the data underwent a

understanding of the ground truth data informed the design

individualized monitoring based on physiological and demographic factors.

artifacts. Missing values were handled using linear interpolation, which estimates a value between two known points by

benchmark of model generalization.
This approach is widely adopted in deep learning research
to balance learning capacity with fair performance assessment.
C. Model Development

and implemented: a baseline Long Short-Term Memory

The baseline LSTM served as the foundation because it is

respiration rate, stress levels, and blood oxygen saturation.
The architecture employed stacked recurrent layers to enhance
representational capacity, while dropout regularization (0.3)

which represent cases correctly identified within the risk level,
and true negatives (TN), which denote correctly identified

IV. RESULTS
A. Ground Truth Data Analysis
The stress level recorded from the Garmin Vivosmart 5
devices was utilized as the ground truth for recognizing heatstress risk states. Table VIII presents descriptive statistics
derived from the ground truth evaluation. Subjective physiological stress varied considerably across the monitoring
period, reflecting the cumulative effect of heat exposure and
physical exertion. Stress levels spanned the full range of 0–99,
with a mean of 49.59 (SD = 28.86), indicating that workers
experienced moderate to high stress at different time points.
Heart rate and heart rate variability also displayed marked
variation, reflecting heterogeneous cardiovascular responses to
heat and exertion. Heart rate ranged from 60 to 129 beats per
minute (mean = 94.45, SD = 20.19), whereas HRV varied

V. DISCUSSION
The results from the baseline LSTM and the attentionaugmented LSTM demonstrate significant improvements in the
prediction of heat stress in construction workers, particularly
under extreme environmental conditions such as those in
Saudi Arabia. This section discusses the implications of these
findings, compares them with existing literature, highlights the
strengths and limitations of the study, and outlines potential
avenues for future work.
A. Comparison with Previous Studies
The baseline LSTM model achieved an accuracy of 93.34%
on the testing dataset, which is consistent with previous studies
that have applied machine learning techniques to occupational health monitoring. In contrast, the proposed attentionenhanced LSTM model achieved a testing accuracy of 95.40%,
while substantially reducing false positives from 4412 to
2450 and false negatives from 4803 to 2400 for low-risk
classification. This improvement is further supported by higher

These comparisons show that the attention-based model

detailed performance metrics for all risk levels, together with

and improved interpretability.
B. Implications for Heat Stress Prediction
The model’s improved precision, recall, and F1 score underscore the potential of attention-augmented LSTM models
to accurately predict heat-related health risks in construction
workers. This improvement is crucial for proactive safety
management because it allows earlier intervention and reduces
the risk of heat-related illness. By focusing on the most critical
time frames in physiological data, the model can provide more
accurate predictions and better support decision-making by
safety personnel.
These results suggest that integrating wearable technology
with advanced machine learning models could become a key
component of future workplace safety strategies, particularly
in high-risk environments. Such a model could help construction companies reduce health-related incidents, improve
worker safety, and enhance overall productivity by minimizing
disruptions due to heat stress.
C. Strengths and Limitations
This study has several strengths. The use of real-time physiological data from wearable devices ensures that the model
is trained on data reflective of actual working conditions. In
addition, the combination of quantitative physiological data
and qualitative self-reported observations allows for a broader
understanding of the factors contributing to heat stress. The
integration of an attention mechanism into the LSTM model
also provides a meaningful enhancement over conventional
sequential learning approaches.
However, the study also has limitations. First, the study
was conducted in a single geographical location, and the
findings may not be directly generalizable to other regions with
different environmental conditions or worker demographics.
Second, the dataset consisted of data from only 19 workers.
While this sample size is sufficient for a proof-of-concept
study, future work with larger and more diverse datasets is

VI. CONCLUSION
Heat stress is a significant occupational risk for construction
workers, particularly in hot climates such as the Middle
East, where prolonged exposure can result in serious health
consequences and impaired productivity. To address this issue,
this study proposed a predictive framework for heat-stress
detection based on Long Short-Term Memory networks enhanced with an attention mechanism. The framework enables
proactive monitoring of physiological signals to anticipate
heat-stress onset and reduce associated risks.
Experimental findings revealed that the proposed attentionbased LSTM model outperformed the baseline LSTM architecture across all evaluated risk states. The baseline
model achieved classification accuracies of 93.34% (low risk),
91.05% (moderate risk), and 92.91% (high risk), while the
attention-based model demonstrated improved accuracies of
96.38%, 95.20%, and 95.90% for the corresponding risk levels.
In addition, the proposed model consistently produced higher
precision, recall, and F1 scores, with values reaching 0.981–
0.997, thereby confirming its superior ability to reduce both
false positives and false negatives.
These results highlight the advantage of incorporating attention mechanisms, which allow the network to focus selectively on the most informative portions of multivariate
time-series data. By capturing complex temporal dependencies
more effectively, the model provides a more robust representation of individualized physiological responses to thermal
load. Beyond technical improvements, this study demonstrates
practical benefits. Coupling wearable physiological monitoring
with attention-based deep learning provides an operational tool
for early detection of heat-related illnesses. Such systems can
enhance worker safety, support compliance with occupational
health regulations, and improve site-level productivity in extreme working environments.
Future research should extend validation across diverse
occupational and environmental contexts to ensure model generalizability. Additional sensor inputs such as hydration levels,
galvanic skin response, and thermal imaging could further
refine predictions and provide a more holistic assessment of
heat stress. Finally, optimizing the framework for deployment
on resource-constrained edge devices will facilitate real-time
inference and decision-making directly in field conditions.

title: Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
text:
Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time
Stochastic Attention
Akash Yadav * 1 Taiwo A. Adebiyi * 1 Ruda Zhang 1
Abstract
Transformer-based scientific foundation models
are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings,
but current architectures give deterministic outputs and provide limited support for calibrated
predictive uncertainty. We propose Stochastic Attention, a lightweight inference-time modification
that randomizes attention by replacing softmax
weights with normalized multinomial samples
controlled by a single concentration parameter,
and produces predictive ensembles without retraining. To set this parameter, we introduce a
calibration objective that matches the stochastic
attention output with the target, yielding an efficient univariate post-hoc tuning problem. We
evaluate this mechanism on two scientific foundation models for weather and timeseries forecasting
along with an additional regression task. Across
benchmarks against uncertainty-aware baselines,
we find that Stochastic Attention achieves the
strongest native calibration and the sharpest prediction intervals at comparable coverage, while
requiring only minutes of post-hoc tuning versus
days of retraining for competitive baselines.
1. Introduction
Scientific modeling has already had to confront an uncomfortable fact: some of its most accurate modern predictors
are mechanistically opaque. Across scientific domains, deep
learning models are no longer viewed merely as flexible
function approximators, but as increasingly useful complements to classical modeling pipelines. In weather forecasting, for example, recent learned systems have shown that
data-driven models can rival, and in some cases surpass,
long-standing forecasting workflows on prominent benchmarks (Fig. 1a) (Nguyen et al., 2023). What this shift has
not yet resolved is how such models should be trusted when
uncertainty matters. If scientific practice is willing to accept
*Equal contribution
1University of Houston, Houston, Texas,
USA. Correspondence to: Ruda Zhang <rudaz@uh.edu>.
Preprint. April 22, 2026.
partially opaque routes to accurate prediction, then uncertainty quantification must confront that same reality rather
than evade it. The challenge is not simply to attach uncertainty to deep models, but to develop forms of uncertainty
that remain useful under the very conditions that make these
models successful: heterogeneous data, noisy and misspecified settings, and internal computations whose strength is
real even when their mechanics are not fully transparent.
That gap is easy to acknowledge in principle, but harder to
formalize in a way that is actually useful. A common intuition is that if predictive distributions look reasonable under
standard scoring rules or if intervals achieve nominal coverage, then uncertainty has been “handled.” We argue that
this view is incomplete. Even in a simple setting such as a
sinusoidal relation, models that recover the same underlying
trend can still express very different kinds of uncertainty:one
may be sharply overconfident, another calibrated but too
diffuse, and a third more usefully balanced (Fig. 1c). This
is not uniquely a scientific-modeling problem; it is a more
general difficulty in uncertainty quantification that becomes
especially consequential in scientific prediction. Useful uncertainty therefore cannot be reduced to a single score. It
lives at the intersection of accuracy, calibration, sharpness,
and cost: a model may be accurate yet systematically overconfident, calibrated yet too diffuse to support action, or
sharp only because it understates risk (Gneiting et al., 2007;
Kuleshov & Deshpande, 2022; Gruber & Buettner, 2022).
This multi-objective structure is precisely what makes uncertainty difficult to reason about, and it helps explain why
the literature has produced many promising tools without a
unifying pattern for what “useful” uncertainty should look
like in practice.
The field has approached this problem from two largely
separate directions. One line of work focuses on how uncertainty is evaluated, relying on proper scores, coverage-based
diagnostics, or calibration metrics as proxies for reliability
(Guo et al., 2017; Gneiting et al., 2007; Lakshminarayanan
et al., 2017). Another focuses on where and how uncertainty
is introduced, through output-level recalibration, weightspace approximations, ensembles, or stochastic forwardpass mechanisms (Guo et al., 2017; Gal & Ghahramani,
2016; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Maddox et al., 2019;
Shen et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2018; Pei et al., 2022). Both

perspectives matter, but neither is sufficient on its own. For
highly parameterized models operating under misspecification, distribution shift, and noisy supervision, useful uncertainty is not guaranteed simply because a standard metric
improves, nor simply because stochasticity has been added
somewhere in the model. This raises a more fundamental
question: if uncertainty is to be useful in transformer-based
models, where should randomness enter, and by what principle should its magnitude be chosen?
We take the view that, for transformer-based scientific foundation models, the natural place to ask that question is the
attention bottleneck. Attention is where contextual information is routed and aggregated, so perturbing it is qualitatively different from only rescaling outputs after prediction
or globally randomizing all model weights. Building on
this perspective, we study inference-time stochastic attention as a lightweight mechanism that introduces controlled
randomness directly into the attention computation while
preserving the deterministic backbone in expectation. Just
as importantly, we do not treat the magnitude of that stochasticity as a free noise knob. Instead, we choose it through a
calibration-oriented criterion, turning stochastic attention
into a calibrated operating point rather than an arbitrary
randomization device.
We investigate this perspective across three settings that
play different roles in the paper. TIMESFM (Das et al.,
2024) serves as a transparent forecasting testbed in which
uncertainty pathologies are visually easy to diagnose. CLIMAX (Nguyen et al., 2023) provides the flagship scientific
forecasting case, where the practical value of calibrated uncertainty is clearest. FT-Transformer regression benchmarks
then broaden the picture beyond the original forecasting domains. Across these settings, our goal is not to argue that a
single lightweight mechanism dominates every alternative
under every scalar score. Rather, we show that introducing
stochasticity at the attention bottleneck identifies a practically useful operating point: one that preserves the strength
of the underlying predictor in expectation, achieves strong
calibration, remains competitive in sharpness once calibration is taken seriously, and does so at substantially lower
cost than retraining-heavy alternatives (Maddox et al., 2019;
Shen et al., 2024; Wilson & Izmailov, 2020; Papamarkou
et al., 2024). Our contributions are threefold:
• We frame uncertainty in scientific foundation models as
a genuinely multi-objective problem governed by accuracy, calibration, sharpness, and cost, and use that lens
to argue that where uncertainty enters a transformer
matters.
• We study inference-time stochastic attention as a
lightweight uncertainty mechanism at the attention
bottleneck and show how its single concentration parameter can be chosen through a calibration-oriented
principle rather than by heuristic tuning.
• We demonstrate across scientific forecasting and regression settings that this yields a strong practical operating point for uncertainty-aware prediction, balancing
calibration, sharpness, and computational efficiency
around strong pretrained or adapted backbones.

Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
2. A lens for evaluating uncertainty in
scientific foundation models
In practice, uncertainty quality is often compressed into one
favored score, one calibration statistic, or one probabilistic
formalism. That compression is convenient, but it obscures
the structure of the problem. What scientists actually need
from uncertainty is more demanding: the central prediction must remain useful, the predictive distribution must
be statistically trustworthy, the reported intervals must be
informative rather than vacuous, and the overall procedure
must remain realistic at the scale of modern transformerbased models. Throughout this paper, we organize that
requirement through four complementary axes: accuracy,
calibration, sharpness, and cost.
2.1. Accuracy, calibration, and sharpness are
complementary
Accuracy, calibration, and sharpness are often invoked together, but they do not collapse into one another. Accuracy
concerns the quality of a representative prediction, typically
the predictive mean or another point summary under a taskrelevant loss. Calibration concerns whether the predictive
distribution is statistically consistent with realized outcomes
in the long run. Sharpness concerns the concentration of that
predictive distribution and therefore whether the reported
uncertainty is informative rather than vacuous (Gneiting
et al., 2007; Kuleshov & Deshpande, 2022).
The key point is not simply that these notions differ, but
that they can pull against one another. A method may retain strong point accuracy while remaining systematically
overconfident. Another may achieve nominal coverage only
by broadening its intervals until they become practically
uninformative. A third may look attractive under a sharpness summary precisely because it understates risk. Figure 1b is meant to make that non-collapse visible: accuracy,
calibration, and sharpness define distinct desiderata, and
improving one of them does not automatically improve the
others. Figure 1c makes the same point in a deliberately
simple setting, where predictors recovering the same underlying sinusoidal relation still express qualitatively different uncertainty—calibrated and sharp but inaccurate, accurate and calibrated but diffuse, accurate and sharp but
miscalibrated, or balanced across all three. In that sense,
uncertainty quality is genuinely multi-objective rather than
reducible to a single scalar target.
This perspective is consistent with the probabilistic forecasting literature, where calibration and sharpness have long
been treated as complementary rather than interchangeable
properties of predictive distributions (Gneiting et al., 2007).
It also clarifies why uncertainty can remain unsatisfying
even when the central prediction is strong: a good mean
forecast is necessary, but it is not enough.
2.2. Cost is part of the decision
For scientific foundation models, cost belongs in the same
coordinate system. This is not a practical footnote added
after the statistical discussion. Uncertainty methods differ
not only in the distributions they induce, but in the training
runs, posterior approximations, checkpoint collections, or
repeated stochastic passes they require. In large-model
settings, those differences can determine whether a method
is realistically usable at all.
That distinction matters because some of the strongest baselines derive their gains from substantial computational investment. Deep ensembles require repeated model training
(Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). SWAG and MultiSWAG
approximate predictive uncertainty through trajectory- or
checkpoint-based posterior structure (Maddox et al., 2019;
Wilson & Izmailov, 2020). Variational Bayesian methods
such as IVON enrich the stochastic training objective, again
at the cost of additional optimization complexity (Shen et al.,
2024). These are meaningful baselines, but they do not
occupy the same operating point as a lightweight inferencetime mechanism. A method that improves a scalar score
only after multiple additional training runs is not solving
the same practical problem as one that achieves useful calibration with minimal internal overhead. Cost therefore
belongs to the uncertainty-design problem itself, not as an
afterthought, but as part of what makes one uncertainty
method practically preferable to another.
2.3. When and where randomness and calibration
happen
Once uncertainty is viewed through these complementary
axes, it becomes natural to ask how current methods actually
intervene. One useful way to organize the landscape is by
when uncertainty or calibration happen and where they act.
The first distinction is temporal. Some methods introduce
uncertainty during training, for example by learning weightspace posteriors or stochastic optimization dynamics that
alter the model itself (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016; Shen et al.,
2024).
Others act at inference time, producing predictive variability through repeated stochastic forward passes,
checkpoint sampling, or architectural stochasticity (Maddox
et al., 2019; Wilson & Izmailov, 2020; Heo et al., 2018;
Pei et al., 2022). A third class leaves the model untouched
and instead calibrates uncertainty after prediction, as in temperature scaling or conformal-style procedures (Guo et al.,
2017; Kuleshov et al., 2018; Vovk et al., 2005; Ye et al.,
2024). The second distinction is structural. Randomness
or calibration may be applied at the output level, in weight
space, or inside the model’s computation.

Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
These choices are not interchangeable. Output-level recalibration can improve uncertainty statistics without changing how the model internally routes information. That is
the logic behind temperature scaling and conformal wrappers: they reshape reported uncertainty after the predictor
has already done its work (Guo et al., 2017; Vovk et al.,
2005). Weight-space methods and ensembles intervene
much more globally, often at substantially higher computational cost, by averaging over parameters, trajectories, or
multiple trained models (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017;
Maddox et al., 2019; Wilson & Izmailov, 2020; Shen et al.,
2024). Stochastic forward-pass approaches sit somewhere in
between, injecting randomness into the network itself while
largely preserving the trained predictor (Gal & Ghahramani,
2016). Within that class, attention-level stochasticity is qualitatively different from indiscriminate perturbation because
it acts at a computational bottleneck that directly governs
how information is routed (Heo et al., 2018; Pei et al., 2022).
Organizing the literature this way does more than tidy up categories. It shows that methods differ not only in strength but
in mechanism: they intervene at different stages of the predictive pipeline and perturb different objects. It also clarifies
a practical point that is often treated as an embarrassment
rather than a fact of current modeling practice. In many
large-model settings, predictive accuracy is established first
and uncertainty is calibrated or attached afterward. We do
not regard that separation as a conceptual failure. The more
relevant question is whether the second-stage uncertainty
mechanism remains tied to the computation in a meaningful
way, rather than merely wrapped around its outputs. That is
the question that motivates the later focus on the attention
bottleneck.
2.4. Proper scores are useful, but not the whole story
This brings us to the role of metrics. Proper scores are valuable because they provide compact summaries of predictive
quality and reward alignment between forecast distributions
and realized outcomes. In practice, however, they are often
asked to do more conceptual work than they can bear. A
lower negative log-likelihood, CRPS, or related score can
reflect improved uncertainty, but it can also reflect increased
spread, altered sharpness, or other changes that are difficult to disentangle directly (Gneiting et al., 2007; Gruber &
Buettner, 2022). In other words, these scores blend together
aspects of uncertainty quality that the present paper is trying
to keep distinct.
That does not make proper scores unimportant. On the
contrary, we report them precisely because they remain informative summaries. But they are not sufficient as the sole
definition of useful uncertainty. A method can improve
a blended score and still land at an undesirable operating
point from the perspective of calibration or practical informativeness. This matters especially in highly parameterized
models operating under misspecification, shift, and noisy supervision, where a predictive distribution can become more
diffuse without becoming more meaningful.
For that reason, we treat proper scores as complementary
to, rather than replacements for, calibration diagnostics.
Throughout the paper, PIT-based diagnostics and coveragebased views play the primary role in assessing probabilistic
consistency, while sharpness summaries and proper scores
help characterize how that calibrated uncertainty is being
achieved. At that point, the next question becomes unavoidable: if useful uncertainty does not follow automatically
either from a single metric or from adding stochasticity
somewhere in the model, then by what principle should the
amount of stochasticity be chosen? Section 3 introduces the
mechanism, and Section 4 turns to that calibration problem
directly.
3. Stochastic attention
If uncertainty is to reflect plausible internal variability rather
than arbitrary perturbation, attention is the natural place to
introduce randomness. Our starting point is that deterministic attention already admits a probabilistic interpretation:
the softmax weights form a simplex-valued distribution over
tokens, and the corresponding attention output is its expectation. Stochastic attention replaces that exact expectation
by a finite-sample approximation drawn from the same categorical distribution. This yields a one-parameter family of
stochastic predictors indexed by a concentration parameter
ν, with small ν producing more dispersed attention outcomes and large ν recovering the deterministic computation.
The construction is probabilistic in a frequentist rather than
fully Bayesian sense: the model parameters remain fixed,
while repeated attention-space sampling induces an implicit
predictive distribution around a frozen transformer.

they define a sample-based joint predictive distribution that

This also makes the scope of the construction precise.
Stochastic attention is introduced only at inference time;
we do not retrain the transformer, and we do not optimize
through discrete samples. The backbone is first trained or
fine-tuned for predictive accuracy, and the attention-space
randomness is calibrated afterward. Accordingly, stochastic
attention should be viewed neither as output-only recalibration nor as posterior inference over all network weights, but
as a post-hoc probabilistic mechanism inside the transformer
computation itself.
Two Monte Carlo quantities play distinct roles. The concentration parameter ν controls the stochastic distribution
itself by determining the amount of attention-space variability within a single forward pass. By contrast, M controls
only how accurately we estimate summaries of the predictive distribution induced by that mechanism. Thus, ν is the
method’s operating parameter, whereas M is simply the
evaluation budget used to estimate predictive summaries.
Taken together, this defines a one-parameter family of
stochastic predictors {fθ,ν}ν∈Ξ around the frozen deterministic backbone fθ, where Ξ ⊆N is the admissible search
domain for ν. The remaining question is how to choose the
operating value of ν.
4. Choosing a calibrated operating point
The concentration parameter ν should be chosen by what we
want the predictive distribution to achieve, not by heuristic
noise tuning. Under the lens of Section 2, useful uncertainty
is not determined by randomness alone, but by a balance
among accuracy, calibration, sharpness, and cost. In scientific settings, that balance is especially consequential:
under-dispersion yields overconfident predictions, while
over-dispersion yields uncertainty that is statistically safer
but operationally uninformative. Both are calibration failures, and both matter in practice.
For that reason, we
treat calibration as the first requirement for selecting the
stochastic-attention operating point. Proper scores remain
useful and are reported later, but they blend calibration with
predictive spread, so the operating point that optimizes a
single scalar score need not be the one with the clearest
probabilistic calibration. Our goal here is therefore not to
re-optimize model parameters, but to choose ν so that the
predictive variability induced by stochastic attention is commensurate with the residual variability observed on held-out
data.

Its scope should nonetheless be stated clearly. We do not
claim that this objective is a universal calibration rule for
all predictive tasks. It is designed for continuous regression
settings, where residual magnitudes and predictive dispersion are naturally compared in a common metric space. It is
therefore best understood as a calibration principle for the
specific one-parameter stochastic family induced by stochastic attention, not as a replacement for all proper scoring rules
or all probabilistic training objectives.
This also clarifies the main design trade-off. A single shared
concentration parameter ν keeps the method lightweight
and easy to calibrate, but it limits expressivity across heads,
layers, coordinates, and inputs. We take that trade-off deliberately here: the goal is not to build the most expressive
possible probabilistic model, but to identify a calibrationfirst operating point that remains simple enough to deploy
while preserving the strength of the deterministic backbone
in expectation.
4.3. Optimization and computational role of ν
In practice, LSA(ν) is evaluated on the held-out calibration
split Dcal. For each candidate ν ∈Ξ, we estimate the
inner expectation using repeated stochastic forward passes
of the frozen model. As in Section 3.3, ν controls the
stochastic predictive distribution induced by attention-space
sampling, whereas the number M of repeated stochastic
forward passes controls only the Monte Carlo accuracy with
which summaries of that distribution are estimated.
When all stochastic attention layers share a single concentration parameter ν, LSA(ν) becomes a one-dimensional
calibration problem. We optimize it using the BO-underuncertainty routine of Yadav & Zhang (2025), which fits a
Bayesian generalized linear model surrogate to noisy evaluations and analytically proposes the next candidate ν; full
details are deferred to the appendix. In practice, each BO
iteration evaluates a single proposed ν on mini-batches from
Dcal using M stochastic forward passes per batch. Combined with the one-dimensional search and analytic BO
suggestion step, this makes ν-selection fast in practice and
far cheaper than retraining-heavy uncertainty baselines.
5. Experimental design
5.1. Models and tasks
The experimental design mirrors the paper’s central premise:
uncertainty quality should be read through several complementary dimensions, and different empirical settings are
useful for different parts of that argument. We therefore
do not present the datasets as interchangeable benchmarks.
TimesFM on the ETT-small datasets (Das et al., 2024) serves
as a diagnostic forecasting setting. It is univariate, visually interpretable, and well suited to showing what underdispersion, over-dispersion, and more useful uncertainty actually look like. In practice, it is also a difficult fine-tuning
regime because the adaptation data are limited, so we use it
primarily as a transparent testbed rather than as the quantitative center of the paper. ClimaX is the flagship scientific
case: a structured, high-dimensional forecasting problem in
which uncertainty must remain meaningful under realistic
scientific demands, and where the practical stakes of calibration are clearest (Nguyen et al., 2023). FT-Transformer on
UCI regression then broadens the scope beyond forecasting,
using the standard Gal-style splits to provide a compact and
reproducible transformer regression setting (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016). Full training, split, and implementation details
are deferred to Appendix C.
5.2. Baselines
In tandem with the established notion that uncertainty methods differ not only in strength, but in where they intervene
and how they generate predictive variability, we compare
against weight-space methods, ensemble-style methods, and
stochastic forward-pass or architectural methods. SWAG
and IVON represent two different routes to weight-space
uncertainty, while MultiSWAG plays the role of a strong
ensemble-style baseline built from repeated SWAG training
runs (Maddox et al., 2019; Wilson & Izmailov, 2020; Shen
et al., 2024). That choice is intentional: MultiSWAG is
not merely another competitor, but a representative of the
broader family of expensive ensemble-based uncertainty
methods that often set a high empirical bar. We also include
MC Dropout as a lightweight stochastic forward-pass baseline (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016), Contextual Dropout as a
stronger context-dependent dropout alternative (Fan et al.,
2021a), and HSA as the closest attention-level stochastic
baseline, since it injects uncertainty inside attention rather
than only through weights or outputs (Pei et al., 2022). Additional baseline summaries are provided in Appendix G.
5.3. Metrics and diagnostics
We report point accuracy, calibration diagnostics, sharpness summaries, and score-based investigations. Point accuracy remains necessary because an uncertainty method that
substantially weakens the underlying predictor loses practical relevance. Calibration is assessed primarily through
PIT behavior, empirical coverage, and, where appropriate,
Wasserstein-1 distance to the uniform distribution. For
scalar targets, PIT is computed from the empirical predictive CDF induced by repeated predictive samples. For
structured outputs such as gridded ClimaX forecasts, PIT
is computed coordinate-wise and then aggregated across
coordinates and test cases; the exact computation for each
setting is given in Appendix C. Under exact probabilistic
calibration, PIT values are uniformly distributed on [0, 1].

5.4. Fairness and cost protocol
The comparison protocol separates native uncertainty quality from post-corrected uncertainty quality. As already emphasized, sharpness is not meaningfully comparable when
calibration differs substantially across methods, making this
distinction essential. The first comparison is therefore always native. Stochastic attention remains native throughout
because its operating point is chosen by a calibration-first
criterion; once that native calibration is established, its sharpness can be interpreted directly in end-to-end comparison.
For baselines whose native predictive distributions are materially miscalibrated, we also report post-scaled comparisons
where appropriate, not to blur the distinction, but to show
what happens once calibration is brought to a more comparable level. This lets later sharpness and score comparisons
be read as differences in uncertainty quality rather than artifacts of obvious under- or over-dispersion as presented in
Sections 6 and 7.
Cost is treated in the same practical spirit. Retraining-heavy
baselines, checkpoint-based ensembles, and lightweight
inference-time mechanisms do not occupy the same deployment regime, even when evaluated on the same task. We
therefore interpret uncertainty quality together with the cost
required to obtain it. This is especially important for the
comparison against strong ensemble-style baselines: their
performance matters, but so does the fact that they achieve
it through repeated training and aggregation rather than
through a lightweight post-hoc mechanism around a frozen
model.

6. Results on scientific forecasting
6.1. TimesFM: a diagnostic view
Before turning to the flagship scientific case, it is useful to
see why calibration-first evaluation matters visually. Figure 2 shows native predictive intervals for all six methods
on one TimesFM case (ETTh1, H=96). SA achieves native coverage of 61.5%, far from the 95% target but already
closer than any baseline (IVON 15.6%, SWAG 16.7%, MultiSWAG 20.8%, Contextual Dropout 19.8%, HSA 38.5%).
Baselines are not merely imperfect; they are systematically
under-dispersed. Narrow intervals that miss most outcomes
are not sharp; they are overconfident. The corresponding equal-coverage visualization, where all baselines are
rescaled to SA’s empirical coverage for a fair sharpness
comparison, is in Appendix E. This is the structure that the
rest of the evaluation must navigate.
6.2. ClimaX: native calibration at the attention
bottleneck
ClimaX is where the calibration-first lens lands most
clearly.
Figure 3a shows native PIT histograms for
all six methods.
SA produces a near-uniform distribution (W1=0.0560); every baseline shows a severely Ushaped PIT: SWAG (0.2195), IVON (0.2132), MultiSWAG
(0.2188), HSA (0.1787), Contextual Dropout (0.1048).
This under-dispersion is not a tuning failure.
We verified that SWAG’s predictive mean is strong: SWAG-mean
reaches ACC=0.9645 and SWAG-BMA reaches 0.9648,
matching the deterministic baseline. Even after a dedicated variance-scale sweep over {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} for
increased predictive spread, the best natively calibrated
SWAG (scale 64) achieves W1=0.116 at coverage 60.9%—
still more than twice SA’s W1 at comparable native coverage
(Appendix D.1).
The SA–HSA comparison is especially informative: both
target the attention bottleneck, but HSA modifies attention
during training and suffers a 22% accuracy degradation
(ACC drops to 0.7476). SA preserves the pretrained spatial
routing by intervening only at inference time, achieving
ACC=0.902 at the BO-optimized ν=4. This is a modest accuracy cost relative to the deterministic baseline (0.964), and
it diminishes rapidly as ν increases: at ν=25, SA reaches
ACC=0.966, essentially matching SWAG-BMA (0.965).
6.3. Calibration, sharpness, and cost
With SA’s native calibration advantage now established, the
question shifts to sharpness, but only once the comparison is fair. Figure 3b shows what happens when baselines
are temperature-scaled: W1 drops to 0.04–0.06 across the
board, confirming that their native under-dispersion was
a correctable calibration failure rather than a fundamental
limitation. SA, which remains native throughout, sits at
W1=0.056, already comparable without any post-hoc adjustment.
With calibration now comparable, sharpness becomes meaningful (Figure 4). SA is the sharpest method overall (normalized mean≈1.0), with MultiSWAG closest at ≈1.02 but
requiring 10 independent training runs. HSA’s accuracy
degradation forces its intervals to 2.74× SA’s width. Table 3
(Appendix D) consolidates the full four-axis comparison:
SA achieves native calibration (W1=0.056) competitive
with post-scaled baselines (0.04–0.06), the sharpest intervals (PI-95 width 1051.9 vs. 1075–2883 for baselines), and
the lowest cost among methods with comparable uncertainty
quality.

7. Results beyond forecasting
The forecasting results establish a strong operating point for
SA, but they leave open whether the mechanism depends
on forecasting structure, LoRA adaptation, or foundationmodel pretraining. Table 2 addresses that question directly:
on eight UCI regression datasets with a from-scratch FTTransformer (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016), SA achieves the
lowest native W1 on 5 of 8 datasets (Panel A), with Naval essentially tied with MC Dropout (0.022 vs. 0.020). After temperature scaling baselines toward comparable coverage, SA
produces the narrowest intervals on 7 of 8 datasets (Panel B).
The exception is Naval, where HSA’s lower point-prediction
error translates into tighter scaled intervals. Per-dataset PIT
histograms and sharpness comparisons for all eight datasets
are in Appendix F; on representative datasets like Yacht
(normalized RMSE=0.05), SA’s PIT is closest to uniform
(W1=0.021) and its intervals remain the sharpest after scaling. Ensemble CRPS evaluated natively (Appendix F.0.1)
confirms that SA is among the two best methods on 4 of 8
datasets, with MultiSWAG winning 5 of 8 through lower
per-sample prediction error from 10 independent training
runs—the same pattern observed on ClimaX.
The UCI results also reveal the method’s operating regime.
SA’s calibration tracks backbone accuracy predictably: on
low-RMSE datasets (Naval 0.04, Yacht 0.05, Energy 0.07),
BO selects high ν (33–76) and the PIT is near-uniform;
as RMSE grows (Kin8nm 0.40, Power Plant 0.24), ν collapses and coverage falls short. On Protein (0.67) and Wine
(0.88), attention-level perturbations cannot span the residual
uncertainty regardless of ν. This limitation is shared by
all post-hoc methods, which degrade when the backbone
is insufficiently accurate. But it defines a clear operating
regime: SA is most valuable around strong pretrained or
well-adapted backbones, precisely the setting scientific foundation models occupy.
8. Discussion
8.1. The calibration–cost trade-off
The empirical picture across three structurally different settings converges on a consistent operating point. SA achieves
strong native calibration, the sharpest or near-sharpest intervals once calibration is comparable, and does so at a fraction
of the cost of retraining-heavy alternatives. These properties
follow from three design choices that reinforce each other:
stochasticity enters only at inference time, preserving the
backbone’s predictive strength; it acts at the attention bottleneck where information is routed rather than at arbitrary
locations; and its magnitude is set by a calibration objective,
turning ν into a principled operating point rather than a free
knob.
The cost comparison sharpens this point.
MultiSWAG
achieves comparable sharpness through 10 independent
training runs whose aggregate compute exceeds SA’s by
over three orders of magnitude. Dropout-based methods
share SA’s inference-time spirit but lack a calibration mechanism tied to the model’s internal computation, leaving them
natively overconfident. HSA targets the same bottleneck but
modifies it during training, disrupting pretrained representations. SA sidesteps all three failure modes by design.
8.2. Limitations of a single-parameter design
One global ν shared across all heads, layers, and coordinates
is what makes SA lightweight, but it also limits expressivity.
The UCI results make this concrete: on datasets where the
backbone is accurate, a single ν suffices for near-uniform
PIT distributions; on noisier tasks where residuals exceed
what attention-level perturbations can induce, calibration sat11

to SA; it is shared by all single-parameter post-hoc calibration methods, from temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017)
to isotonic recalibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018), which similarly trade expressivity for simplicity and robustness.
Extending to layer-dependent or input-dependent ν is natural but involves a genuine trade-off: each degree of freedom
increases expressivity at the cost of calibration complexity
and overfitting risk. The present results suggest that the
simplest version already identifies a useful operating point
for the strong-backbone regime where scientific foundation
models operate.
8.3. Uncertainty and computational structure
Beyond the practical trade-offs above, the results point to
a qualitative distinction worth making explicit. The uncertainty SA produces is not sensitivity to parameter perturbation or random subnetwork selection; it is sensitivity to
how the model allocates computational resources across
tokens. That this form of variability, tied directly to the
model’s internal information routing, already delivers better
calibration at lower cost suggests that aligning the source
of stochasticity with the model’s computational structure is
itself a useful inductive bias for uncertainty quantification.
9. Conclusion
We introduced inference-time stochastic attention, a mechanism that replaces exact attention expectations with finitesample multinomial draws controlled by a single concentration parameter ν. Choosing ν through a calibration objective
yields predictive distributions that are well calibrated natively, competitive in sharpness at comparable coverage, and
obtainable without retraining.
Across ClimaX weather forecasting, TimesFM time-series
prediction, and FT-Transformer tabular regression, SA
consistently achieves the strongest native calibration and
the sharpest intervals on a coverage-comparable basis, requiring only inference-time passes on a frozen backbone.
Under proper scoring rules, a different operating point
(ν=25) ranks first, confirming that calibration-first and
score-optimal evaluations are complementary. The main
limitation mirrors the main simplification: a single global
ν bounds expressivity when the backbone itself is insufficiently accurate. Extensions to richer parameterizations
remain a natural next step, but the simplest version already
identifies a practically useful operating point for uncertainty
in scientific foundation models.

C. Experimental Setup and Reproducibility Details
This appendix section summarizes the experimental settings used in the paper and provides the key implementation details
needed to reproduce the reported uncertainty diagnostics. We consider three evaluation settings: (i) transformer-based
time-series forecasting with TIMESFM, (ii) global weather forecasting with CLIMAX, and (iii) UCI regression as a compact
testbed for evaluating calibration and sharpness beyond the scientific forecasting examples. Baseline-method summaries are
given separately in Appendix G.
C.1. TimesFM: Architecture and Forecasting
Backbone.
TIMESFM is a decoder-only transformer for time-series forecasting that operates on non-overlapping input
patches (Das et al., 2024). Each patch is mapped to a token representation and processed by stacked causal self-attention
layers. Forecasts are decoded in output patches and extended autoregressively for longer horizons. Unless otherwise stated,
deterministic reporting uses the point-forecast decoding head. TimesFM supports multiple decoding heads; for deterministic
reporting we use the point-forecast head (decode index = 5).
Datasets and splits.
We evaluate on the ETT-small benchmarks ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, and ETTm2 (Zhou et al., 2021),
using the standard Informer split boundaries: ETTh*: training 0–8640, validation 8640–11520, test 11520–14400; ETTm*:
training 0–34560, validation 34560–46080, test 46080–57600. Following our adaptation protocol, normalization statistics
are computed on the full training segment, while model adaptation uses only the first 10% of the training portion. Each
column is treated as an independent univariate series.
Forecasting protocol and metric.
We use context length 512 and forecasting horizons of 96 and 192. Forecasting is
performed autoregressively in patch units. Predictive accuracy is reported using MAE, averaged across series and forecast
horizon.

Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
Lightweight task adaptation.
To obtain a strong deterministic checkpoint while keeping the pretrained backbone fixed,
we use LoRA adapters attached to the query–key–value projection, attention output projection, and the two linear layers in
the feed-forward block. All pretrained backbone parameters are frozen and only LoRA parameters are trained.
C.2. ClimaX: Architecture and Global Forecasting Protocol
Backbone.
CLIMAX is a ViT-style foundation model for gridded weather and climate fields (Nguyen et al., 2023). It
tokenizes each variable field into spatial patches, aggregates variable information through cross-attention, and processes the
resulting token sequence with a ViT backbone.
Task and metrics.
We evaluate global forecasting at a 72-hour lead time. Deterministic predictive accuracy is reported
using latitude-weighted MSE, latitude-weighted RMSE, and latitude-weighted anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC),
following the standard evaluation protocol for CLIMAX.
Model adaptation.
We start from the pretrained 5.625◦checkpoint and use LoRA adapters on the attention projections
and MLP linear layers. The pretrained backbone is frozen, while normalization layers remain trainable. Best and final
checkpoints are selected using validation latitude-weighted RMSE.
C.3. UCI Regression Benchmarks
Purpose.
In addition to the forecasting experiments, we evaluate stochastic attention on standard UCI regression tasks
to test whether the method extends beyond the two scientific foundation-model case studies. This provides a compact
regression setting in which calibration, sharpness, and proper scoring rules can be compared across multiple datasets under a
common protocol.
Evaluation protocol.
For each UCI dataset, we begin with a deterministic transformer-based regressor and then apply the
same post-hoc stochastic-attention calibration procedure used in the main paper. We report deterministic predictive accuracy,
along with uncertainty diagnostics based on PIT, empirical coverage, interval width, and, where applicable, proper scoring
rules. Native and post-scaled comparisons are reported separately in the appendix results.
C.4. Predictive Samples for Calibration Diagnostics
All uncertainty methods considered in the paper induce predictive distributions through samples. To unify evaluation across
methods, we form an empirical predictive distribution bF from repeated predictive samples for each test case. PIT values are
then computed from bF for scalar outcomes, and coordinate-wise for structured outputs, aggregating over coordinates when
needed.
Stochastic attention.
For stochastic attention, each predictive sample corresponds to a single stochastic forward pass
of the frozen model, with attention rows sampled according to Algorithm 1. The concentration parameter ν is calibrated
on held-out data using Algorithm 2, after which repeated stochastic forward passes are used to estimate calibration and
sharpness diagnostics.
SWAG-LoRA and MultiSWAG.
For SWAG-LoRA, predictive samples are obtained by sampling LoRA weights from the
SWAG approximation and performing one forward pass per draw. For MultiSWAG, samples are aggregated across multiple
independently trained SWAG-LoRA models, yielding a mixture approximation.
IVON-LoRA.
For IVON-LoRA, predictive samples are generated by sampling LoRA weights from the learned Gaussian
variational approximation and running one forward pass per sample.

G. Baseline Method Summaries
This appendix section summarizes the baseline uncertainty methods used in the experiments. The baselines were selected to represent different mechanisms for producing predictive uncertainty in fine-tuned transformer models: stochastic
forward passes induced by dropout, weight-space posterior approximations, mixtures of posterior approximations, variational/Bayesian training, and stochastic architectural perturbations. This organization is useful because stochastic attention
is best understood not only as another competing uncertainty method, but as a method that occupies a different point in the
design space of where randomness is introduced and when calibration is performed.

G.2. Contextual Dropout
Contextual dropout generalizes standard dropout by making the dropout distribution depend on the input covariates, rather
than using a single global dropout distribution shared across all samples (Fan et al., 2021b). In the paper’s Bayesian
interpretation, the dropout masks become data-dependent local random variables, so different inputs induce different
distributions over the effective network weights.

G.6. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
LoRA fine-tunes a pre-trained model by freezing its original weights and introducing a low-rank parameterization for the
weight update in selected linear layers (Hu et al., 2022). Concretely, for a pre-trained weight matrix W0 ∈Rd×k, LoRA
reparameterizes the adapted weight as
W = W0 + ∆W,
∆W = BA,
(40)
where B ∈Rd×r and A ∈Rr×k with rank r ≪min(d, k). The pre-trained weights W0 are held fixed, and only the LoRA
parameters (A, B) are trained. For an input x, the resulting forward pass is
h = Wx = W0x + BAx.
(41)
LoRA commonly scales the update by α/r, yielding h = W0x + α
r BAx, and initializes A with a small random matrix
while setting B = 0 so that ∆W = 0 at initialization.
G.7. SWAG-LoRA, MultiSWAG-LoRA, and IVON-LoRA
We implement SWAG-LoRA and MultiSWAG-LoRA by combining the SWA/SWAG and MultiSWAG procedures described
above with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022; Izmailov et al., 2018; Maddox et al., 2019; Onal et al., 2024). The core SWAG and
MultiSWAG constructions remain unchanged; the key difference is that the posterior approximation is placed only over
the trainable LoRA adapters rather than over the full set of model weights. This restriction is what makes the Bayesian
treatment computationally feasible for large pre-trained models.
Let ϕ denote the vector of trainable LoRA parameters (i.e., the collection of all (A, B) matrices included in our LoRA
configuration). In SWAG-LoRA, we keep the pre-trained backbone weights fixed and apply SWA/SWAG to ϕ, constructing
the same diagonal-plus-low-rank Gaussian approximation but over the LoRA parameter trajectory. At inference, we sample
ϕ, insert the sampled LoRA parameters into the model (leaving the backbone unchanged), and average predictions across
samples, using the same batch-norm refresh convention as SWAG when applicable. This avoids the substantially more
expensive task of estimating a posterior over all network parameters.
MultiSWAG-LoRA follows the same extension as MultiSWAG: we build multiple independent SWAG-LoRA components
from separate runs (e.g., different random seeds/initializations) and average predictions across components and samples,
yielding Bayesian marginalization across multiple basins while remaining in LoRA parameter space. In practice, this is
often implemented as “L SWAG solutions, M samples per solution,” producing an ensemble of size L × M, with the same
batch-norm refresh convention as SWAG when applicable.
We also implement IVON-LoRA by replacing the standard LoRA optimizer (e.g., AdamW) with the IVON variationallearning procedure on the LoRA parameters, while keeping the backbone fixed (Shen et al., 2024; Cong et al., 2024).
Thus, the variational posterior is placed directly over ϕ rather than fit post hoc after training, and the diagonal posterior
variance is learned through IVON’s scale/curvature vector during optimization. This makes IVON-LoRA a direct Bayesian
optimizer over the LoRA adapters, with only minor extra cost from posterior sampling during training. At evaluation time,
we either use the variational mean (IVON-LoRA@mean) or approximate the posterior predictive by averaging predictions
over multiple samples ϕ(m) ∼q(ϕ) (IVON-LoRA), analogously to the sampling-based predictions described for IVON.
G.8. Hierarchical Stochastic Attention (HSA)
Hierarchical stochastic attention (HSA) injects randomness directly into transformer self-attention through Gumbel-Softmax
sampling (Pei et al., 2022). The reference paper first introduces a simpler stochastic-attention-over-values variant, then
extends it hierarchically by forcing key heads to stochastically attend to a set of learnable centroids before attending to
values. This makes HSA particularly relevant in our study because, like stochastic attention, it perturbs the attention pathway
itself rather than only randomizing weights or activations.

Abstract
This technical note revisits the relationship between RaBitQ and TurboQuant under a unified comparison framework. We compare the two methods in terms of methodology, theoretical guarantees, and empirical performance, using a reproducible, transparent, and symmetric setup. Our
results show that, despite the claimed advantage of TurboQuant, TurboQuant does not provide a consistent improvement over RaBitQ in directly
comparable settings; in many tested configurations, it performs worse than
RaBitQ. We further find that several reported runtime and recall results
in the TurboQuant paper could not be reproduced from the released implementation under the stated configuration.
Overall, this note clarifies
the shared structure and genuine differences between the two lines of work,
while documenting reproducibility issues in the experimental results reported by the TurboQuant paper.

Introduction
Vector quantization in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces has become a fundamental problem in modern AI systems, including vector databases and large language model (LLM)
serving.
In these settings, the goal of quantization is to (1) reduce memory usage by
compressing high-dimensional vector data; (2) reduce computational costs related to the
vectors; and (3) preserve the geometric quantities needed by downstream tasks, especially
inner products.
Recently, TurboQuant, first posted on arXiv in April 2025 and later accepted at ICLR
2026 1, has drawn substantial public attention through claims such as “at least 6x memory
reduction and up to 8x speedup, all with zero accuracy loss” (Zandieh et al., 2025a; Zandieh
& Mirrokni, 2026). However, these public-facing claims are framed primarily against an
uncompressed baseline, and thus, do not by themselves explain how TurboQuant should be
understood relative to prior quantization methods.
One of the most directly relevant prior methods is RaBitQ. The original 1-bit RaBitQ
was submitted to SIGMOD 2024 in October 2023, accepted, and posted on arXiv in May
2024 (Gao & Long, 2024); its multi-bit extension was posted on arXiv in September 2024
1https://openreview.net/forum?id=tO3ASKZlok
arXiv:2604.19528v1 [cs.LG] 21 Apr 2026

and later accepted at SIGMOD 2025 (Gao et al., 2025b). TurboQuant and RaBitQ are
closely related: the two lines overlap in application scenarios, share important method-level
structure, and emphasize closely related theoretical guarantees. Yet the TurboQuant paper
does not provide an accurate and balanced account of that relationship in three respects.
At the method level, RaBitQ is not described or compared with sufficient accuracy. At the
theory level, some characterizations of RaBitQ’s theoretical guarantees are factually incorrect and unsupported. At the experimental level, the setup used for the RaBitQ baseline
is not fully disclosed; subsequent email correspondence reveals that the baseline was run
under conditions highly unfavorable to RaBitQ.
This technical note is written to address this gap. Our purpose is to place RaBitQ and
TurboQuant within a single comparison framework and to characterize precisely what is
shared, what is genuinely different, and what conclusions about theory and experiments
are justified under a reproducible, transparent and symmetric standard. The report serves
two purposes simultaneously: it provides a citable technical comparison and it offers a clear
answer to the broader public question of how RaBitQ and TurboQuant are actually compared to each other. Our experimental comparison further shows that the empirical claims
in the TurboQuant paper are difficult to reconcile with reproducible evaluations using the
released artifacts. In directly comparable inner-product estimation and nearest-neighbor
search settings, TurboQuant does not consistently improve over RaBitQ; in many tested
configurations, it performs worse. For quantization time, we find that the reported TurboQuant results cannot be reproduced from the released implementation under the stated
hardware configuration, with our measured running times differing substantially from the
reported numbers. We also observe inconsistencies between the reported and reproduced
RaBitQ recall and runtime results. These discrepancies indicate that the reported experimental results in the TurboQuant paper are not reproducible from the released artifacts
under the stated experimental configuration. In addition, the undisclosed use of asymmetric hardware and parallelism settings for the RaBitQ baseline further weakens the reported
comparison as evidence of a consistent empirical advantage over RaBitQ.
We emphasize that this note is not intended to provide a comprehensive survey or benchmark of vector quantization methods in vector databases, LLM serving systems, or broader
application domains 2. It focuses exclusively on the overlap between RaBitQ and TurboQuant and on establishing how they should be compared on common technical ground.
Both methods involve several versions of practical implementations; in the technical note,
we specify the version in detail for transparency. We also provide code for reproducing all
experimental results in this report to facilitate independent evaluation. Throughout this
note, we use RaBitQ to refer to the current RaBitQ line of work, including the original
1-bit RaBitQ (Gao & Long, 2024), its multi-bit extension (Gao et al., 2025b), its GPU
version (Shi et al., 2026), and the optimized implementations in the RaBitQ Library (Gao
et al., 2025a).3
The remainder of this note is organized as follows. We first compare the methodology of
both methods under the same comparison framework, followed by a symmetric comparison
of their theoretical claims. We next examine the experimental setup and baseline disclosure
issues relevant to their reported empirical comparison. We conclude with what we believe
is the most accurate characterization of the relationship between the two lines of work.

a central goal is to preserve inner products between vectors 4.
A quantization algorithm operates in two stages. In the quantization stage, each input data
vector is mapped to a compact representation called a quantization code. In the estimation
stage, the quantization code is used to estimate the inner product between the data vector
and an arbitrary query vector.
The performance of a quantization algorithm is usually evaluated along five dimensions:
(1) quantization time, (2) space consumption, (3) accuracy of inner-product estimation, (4)
inner-product estimation time, and (5) theoretical guarantees. Throughout the paper, ∥· ∥
denotes the ℓ2 norm unless otherwise specified.
2.2
Methodology
In their original papers and artifacts, RaBitQ and TurboQuant are described using different
terminology. To compare the two methods clearly, we describe the algorithmic procedures of
both RaBitQ and TurboQuant under the same framework. A summary comparison between
RaBitQ and TurboQuant is provided in Table 1.
2.2.1
Preprocessing of Both RaBitQ and TurboQuant.
Both RaBitQ and TurboQuant encode the norm and direction of a vector separately. In
practice, once the norm is stored, the core quantization procedure of each method focuses
on quantizing the normalized vector.
Both RaBitQ and TurboQuant apply a random rotation, which is a form of Johnson–
Lindenstrauss Transformation (Johnson & Lindenstrauss, 1984), as the first step for all
vectors. Both methods use the distributional information of vectors after random rotation
to design their quantization algorithms.
Specifically, both methods sample and store a
random rotation matrix, and apply the same random rotation to all vectors. In the following
sections, without further specification, we assume that all vectors have been rotated by this
random matrix.

2.2.4
Quantization of TurboQuant.
The TurboQuant method includes two variants: one optimized for vector reconstruction and
the other for unbiased inner-product estimation.
For vector reconstruction, TurboQuant constructs a scalar codebook according to the Lloyd–
Max condition. Specifically, after normalization and random rotation, the coordinates of a
rotated vector follow the distribution induced by the uniform spherical measure, as characterized in (Khokhlov, 2006). For a target bit-width of B, TurboQuant constructs a scalar
codebook with 2B centroids by solving the corresponding one-dimensional continuous kmeans problem under this distribution. Each coordinate is then quantized to the index of
its nearest centroid, and the compressed representation stores these centroid indices for all
coordinates. Note that it can compute the reconstructed vector, denoted by ¯x, by looking-up
the codebook based on the stored indices.
For inner-product estimation, TurboQuant introduces a residual-correction stage. Given a
total budget of B bits per coordinate, it first applies (B −1) bits to obtain a reconstruction,

Comparison of Theoretical Guarantees
In this section, we compare in detail the theoretical guarantees of RaBitQ and TurboQuant
on inner-product estimation.
We focus on the inner-product-oriented variant of each method, since the reconstructionoriented variant is optimized for reconstruction error and does not provide unbiased innerproduct estimation.
Under this scope, both RaBitQ and TurboQuant provide unbiased
estimators of the inner product between unit vectors.
We first note that both RaBitQ and TurboQuant are randomized algorithms whose estimation error is a random variable. Rather than providing a deterministic guarantee, both
methods can provide a probabilistic guarantee: the additive error of inner product between
unit vectors is bounded by ϵ with probability at least 1 −δ, where ϵ, δ ∈(0, 1). The key
quantity of interest is therefore the trade-off among the error bound ϵ, the failure probability
δ, and the bit-width B.
In 2017, Alon and Klartag (Alon & Klartag, 2017) established the optimal trade-off for
approximate inner-product sketches under additive-error guarantees, providing matching
upper and lower bounds on the bit-width B required to ensure that the additive error of
inner-product estimation between unit vectors is bounded by ϵ with probability at least
1 −δ. Specifically, as adapted from the proof of Theorem 4.1 in (Alon & Klartag, 2017),

If one applies Chebyshev’s inequality to this variance bound, the resulting

Comparison of Experimental Results
We follow the TurboQuant paper and evaluate RaBitQ and TurboQuant in the following
aspects: namely (1) quantization accuracy, (2) quantization efficiency, (3) nearest neighbor
search.
It is important to note that the efficiency of inner-product estimation is also a
key evaluation criterion for quantization methods. RaBitQ supports efficient inner-product
estimation through a combination of algorithmic and system-level techniques, including
bitwise operations (Gao & Long, 2024), FastScan (Andr´e et al., 2017), and incremental estimation (Gao et al., 2025b). In contrast, the publicly released TurboQuant codebase only
provides a conceptual Python implementation for inner-product estimation, rather than
an optimized implementation suitable for efficiency benchmarking.
Under these circumstances, a fair empirical comparison of estimation efficiency is not possible. We therefore
do not include such efficiency experiments in this report. We also attempted to reproduce
the KV-cache results reported for TurboQuant based on the publicly available materials
in OpenReview. However, those materials are incomplete for the LLM experiments and
therefore do not support a reliable reproduction of the reported results. We will continue
our reproduction efforts and update this report if we are able to resolve the remaining
implementation issues and complete the evaluation.
For TurboQuant, we use the PyTorch implementation made available on OpenReview 5. For
RaBitQ, we use by default the C++ implementation open-sourced in the RaBitQ library 6,
with the faster quant flag disabled and a random orthogonal matrix for vector rotation
(consistent with TurboQuant). We note that faster RaBitQ implementations are available
in the same library; we use this configuration for reproducibility, as the TurboQuant paper
compares against a Python counterpart of it.
We use a cloud instance with Nvidia A100 GPU (80 GiB VRAM) and 16 VCPUs by following
the original setup of the papers and a dual-socket server equipped with two Intel Xeon Gold
6418H processors (48 cores / 96 threads in total). For the reproducibility, we compile all
the source codes we use for the experiments in this paper here: https://github.com/
VectorDB-NTU/rabitq-turboquant-comparison.

Quantization Efficiency
Following the TurboQuant paper, we use three datasets including GloVe-200 (200dimensional) and two DBpedia Entities datasets (1536-dimensional and 3072-dimensional).
Specifically, we sample 100,000 vectors from each dataset and quantize the sampled vectors
with 4 bits per dimension.
For RaBitQ, we test four implementations, namely (1) RaBitQ: which is the default implementation with the faster quant flag disabled and a random orthogonal matrix for vector
rotation (consistent with TurboQuant), (2) RaBitQfastOn-FHT, which is a faster implementation of RaBitQ with the faster quant flag enabled and Fast Hadamard Transform (FHT)
from the FFHT Library (Andoni et al., 2015) and ideas in Kac’s Walk (Jain et al., 2022) for

of RaBitQ and (4) RaBitQfastOn-FHT (GPU), which is the GPU version of RaBitQ with the
faster quant flag enabled and uses FHT and ideas in Kac’s Walk for faster vector rotation.
For RaBitQ, we use it for reproducibility consideration since the TurboQuant paper implements a Python version of this implementation and uses it for evaluating the performance
of RaBitQ. For RaBitQ (GPU), we use it for a more direct comparison with TurboQuant
since the TurboQuant implementation runs on GPU. We collect the running time of the
methods, with the time for rotating the vectors included. For GPU-based implementations,

RaBitQ is faster than TurboQuant on the same hardware.
When compared on
the same hardware (i.e., GPU), RaBitQ is substantially faster than TurboQuant.
The

4.3
Nearest Neighbor Search
Following the TurboQuant paper, we use three datasets, namely GloVe-200, OpenAI3-1536,
and OpenAI3-3072. For each dataset, we construct a base set and a query set. For OpenAI31536 and OpenAI3-3072, the base set has 100,000 vectors and the query set contains 1,000
vectors. For GloVe-200, we sample a subset of 100,000 vectors from the original corpus as
the base set and use the provided query set of 10,000 vectors. Following the TurboQuant
paper, for all three datasets, we use the inner product of normalized vectors as the metric
for nearest neighbor search.
We compare RaBitQ, namely RaBitQprod, with the two TurboQuant variants, namely
TurboQuantprod and TurboQuantmse.
Note that we exclude RaBitQmse from this comparison as it is not designed for inner-product estimation, which is the objective underlying
nearest neighbor search. On the other hand, we include both variants of TurboQuant in the
comparison for transparency as the TurboQuant paper did not specify the version they used
in the experiment. For each method, we first quantize the vectors in the base set and then

title: Revisiting RaBitQ and TurboQuant: A Symmetric Comparison of Methods, Theory, and Experiments
text:

Our results, by contrast, are averaged over 10 independent runs with standard deviations reported, and are fully reproducible from the code provided in our repository. These reproduced results do not support the TurboQuant paper’s conclusion that TurboQuant consistently outperforms RaBitQ in nearest neighbor search.

Conclusion
This note has examined the relationship between RaBitQ and TurboQuant across three
dimensions: methodology, theoretical guarantees, and empirical performance.
At the method level, both RaBitQ and TurboQuant apply a random rotation as their first
step and exploit the resulting distributional properties to design their respective quantization
schemes as well as analyzing the unbiasedness and error bounds for inner product estimation.
At the theoretical level, RaBitQ provably achieves the asymptotically optimal spacedistortion trade-off established by Alon and Klartag (Alon & Klartag, 2017), with a bitwidth that grows with the failure probability δ at the rate of log log(1/δ). TurboQuant,
by contrast, provides only a variance guarantee on its estimator. Converting this to a tail
bound via Chebyshev’s inequality yields a dependence that grows as log(1/δ), which is
exponentially worse than the optimal rate.
At the experimental level, our reproducible evaluation shows that TurboQuant offers no
clear and consistent advantage over RaBitQ in directly comparable settings. In quantization
accuracy, RaBitQprod matches or outperforms TurboQuantprod across all tested bit widths.
In quantization efficiency, RaBitQ is substantially faster than TurboQuant on the same
hardware, and its CPU implementation is competitive with TurboQuant on an A100 GPU. In
nearest neighbor search, RaBitQ consistently achieves higher recall than both TurboQuant
variants across all datasets and bit widths. Furthermore, we find that the runtime and
recall results reported in the TurboQuant paper could not be reproduced from the released
implementation under the stated hardware configuration.
We hope this note serves as a useful and citable reference for researchers working on vector
quantization, and that the symmetric comparison framework presented here contributes to
a more accurate understanding of the relationship between the two methods.
